title: Controlling quantum transport by measurement-rate modulation
abstract: Temporal modulation of the measurement rate provides a powerful mechanism for controlling open-system dynamics through measurement backaction. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal exactly solvable model of a continuously monitored quantum particle on a switching lattice. We derive exact analytical expressions for the long-time current under both periodic and stochastic switching, revealing a common slow-switching limit and identifying a measurement-induced crossover between Zeno- and anti-Zeno-dominated transport regimes that controls the direction of the current.
summary:
This paper demonstrates that modulating the rate at which a quantum particle is measured can be used as a control knob to induce directed current flow in an otherwise symmetric system. By analyzing both periodic and stochastic switching protocols, the authors show that breaking the symmetry of measurement rates ($\delta R 
eq 0$) is necessary for non-zero transport. The work provides deep insights into the interplay between coherent dynamics, dissipation, and measurement backaction.
main_problem: The research addresses how controlling open-system dynamics and stationary quantum transport can be achieved by temporally modulating the measurement rate (measurement backaction).
main_result:
Directed particle transport is only possible when the measurement rate is modulated ($\delta R 
eq 0$), as this breaks the dynamical symmetry of the system.
method: The authors derive exact analytical expressions for the long-time current using methods applicable to both periodic and stochastic switching protocols, including solving coupled linear differential equations.
model_or_system: The model is a minimal exactly solvable quantum particle on a 1D lattice that undergoes continuous monitoring. The dynamics are governed by a master equation incorporating coherent tunneling, incoherent hopping, and measurement-induced dephasing terms whose rates switch between two values ($R^+$ and $R^-$).
key_observables: Long-time averaged particle velocity ($v_\infty$), which serves as the primary diagnostic for directed transport.
important_parameters: The difference in measurement rates ($\delta R = (R^+ - R^-)/2$) is crucial; the analysis also explores limits like slow-switching and fast-driving regimes.
main_assumptions: For stochastic switching, the system is assumed to be ergodic. For periodic switching, convergence to an asymptotic state is assumed.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the lattice structure for different switching states; Figure 2 plots $v_\infty$ versus driving parameters (period or rate); Figures 3 and 4 map out transport regimes separating Zeno-dominated from anti-Zeno-dominated transport regions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general dynamics using a master equation for a switching lattice. It then derives analytical solutions for the long-time current under periodic driving, followed by an analysis using the Birkhoff ergodic theorem for stochastic switching. Finally, it compares results across different time/driving limits.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete theoretical tools to engineer non-equilibrium quantum transport in open systems, directly relevant to controlling quantum dynamics using measurement backaction, a key area in quantum optics and AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of the lattice for the two possible values of the time-dependent lattice configuration s(t). The lattice consists of equally spaced sites separated by a distance L. Coherent tunneling (red double-headed ar- rows) couples the two sites within each dimer (2j, 2j + 1) with tunneling rate ω, whereas incoherent hopping (blue ar- rows) connects neighboring dimers with transition rate Γ. For s(t) = +1, hopping proceeds from site 2j −1 to site 2j, whereas for s(t) = −1 the hopping direction is reversed. The two configurations therefore favor transport in opposite direc- tions.

FIG. 3. Transport-regime diagram for the periodic proto- col. Black curves are contour lines of the dimensionless long- time averaged velocity v∞/(ωL). The thick solid curves in- dicate the zero-current boundaries (v∞= 0). The cyan- shaded region denotes the anti-Zeno-dominated transport regime (κ > 0), while the unshaded region corresponds to the Zeno-dominated regime (κ < 0), with the two regimes separated by the boundary κ = 0. (a) Dependence on ωT and R−/ω for Γ/ω = 0.5. (b) Dependence on Γ/ω and R−/ω for ωT = 2. In both panels, R+/ω = 2.

FIG. 2. Dimensionless long-time averaged velocity v∞/(ωL) as a function of (a) ωT for the periodic protocol and (b) 2ω/γ for the stochastic protocol. Whereas the stochastic protocol preserves the transport direction for all switching rates, the periodic protocol exhibits a current reversal as the switching period decreases, signaling a crossover from Zeno- to anti-Zeno-dominated transport. The curves correspond to R+/ω = 2, R−/ω = 0.2, and Γ/ω = 0.5 (brown dashed), 1 (blue dash-dotted), and 2 (red solid). The horizontal gray dash-dotted line indicates zero current, while the colored dot- ted lines denote the asymptotic slow-switching limit.

FIG. 4. Transport-regime diagram in the (ωT, Γ/ω) plane for the periodic protocol, corresponding to the parameters R+/ω = 2 and R−/ω = 0.2. Black curves are contour lines of the dimensionless long-time averaged velocity v∞/(ωL). The thick solid curve indicates the zero-current boundary (v∞= 0). The cyan-shaded region denotes the anti-Zeno- dominated transport regime (κ > 0), while the unshaded re- gion corresponds to the Zeno-dominated regime (κ < 0); the boundary is defined by κ = 0.
